pois.short_description: The 1941 art moderne flagship of the Brooklyn Public Library system at Grand Army Plaza, shaped like an open book; holds the Brooklyn Collection and the complete Brooklyn Eagle archive.

beats.script_body: Artists from Walt Whitman to Spike Lee have drawn inspiration from Brooklyn. The Dutch settled it in 1636 and named it Breuckelen, and it stayed an independent city until 1898, when it was incorporated as a borough of New York. In the years that followed, everyone from New England farmers to European immigrants put down roots in what was then a rural swath of land, now covering around seventy-one square miles. Brooklyn still draws immigrants from all over the world, making it one of the most diverse places in the United States.

beats.source_passage: Artists from Walt Whitman to Spike Lee have drawn inspiration from dynamic Brooklyn. Settled by the Dutch in 1636 and named Breuckelen, it was an independent city until 1898, when it was incorporated as a borough of New York. In the ensuing years, everyone from New England farmers to European immigrants put down roots in this rural swath of land, now occupying around 71 square miles (184 sq km). Brooklyn still attracts immigrants from all over the world, making it one of the most diverse places in the United States and a great place to explore the cuisines and traditions of other cultures.

beats.script_body: One of the engineering marvels of the nineteenth century, the Brooklyn Bridge was the world's first steel suspension bridge, completed in 1883, and it overawed onlookers with its sheer size. Awe-inspiring it was, but also serviceable: in 1884, circus-founder P. T. Barnum paraded over it with twenty-one elephants to demonstrate that it was safe. Today the bridge inspired both architect Frank Lloyd Wright and artist Georgia O'Keeffe, and crossing it on foot takes about forty-five minutes over its six-thousand-foot span.

beats.script_body: The Brooklyn Bridge was the first-ever bridge to link Manhattan Island to a populous outer borough, and like so many fabled structures, it is supposed to be cursed. Designer John Augustus Roebling died from injuries sustained while taking measurements for the towers. His son Washington was crippled by the bends while overseeing underwater work, but, determined to continue, he supervised the project from afar by watching through a telescope. Opened in 1883, it was the world's longest span for more than twenty years.

beats.script_body: Few New York neighborhoods rival Brooklyn Heights for its historic buildings. Some of the borough's first brick houses and brownstones were built here after 1814, when regular ferry service between Manhattan and Brooklyn was established. Designated New York's first historic district in 1965, the neighborhood has since been protected from invasive development, and a walk down Willow Street reveals some of the handsomest and most architecturally diverse buildings in the city.

beats.script_body: One of the most picturesque and romantic spots in the city, this promenade is perched high above the East River and the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, with lovely views of the harbor, Lower Manhattan, and the Brooklyn Bridge. Stretching for a third of a mile between Remsen and Orange Streets, it draws everyone from tourists and old-timers to teenage couples and families. Completed in 1950 under the influential city builder Robert Moses, the promenade was created in part to appease residents who opposed the construction of the BQE. The design works surprisingly well; even the noise of cars whizzing below is soothing, calling to mind rushing water more than traffic.

beats.script_body: A horticultural triumph, the fifty-two-acre Brooklyn Botanic Garden has been one of the borough's great attractions since 1910. Immaculately maintained and home to wild rabbits, ducks, and turtles, it seems instantly to induce a state of calm. Among its highlights are more than two hundred cherry trees, which blossom in April. Set among rolling hills, the Japanese Hill-and-Pond Garden incorporates traditional elements such as a Shinto shrine by the pond, overhung with evergreen trees that make it a truly meditative spot.

beats.script_body: The crown jewel of Brooklyn's sixty-branch library system, the majestic Central Library sits just steps from the Brooklyn Botanic Garden. Constructed in 1941 in contemporary art moderne style, a variant of art deco, the building resembles an open book: the spine faces Grand Army Plaza, while its two wings open like book covers along Eastern Parkway and Flatbush Avenue. The grand entrance and plaza make a pleasant backdrop for a free summer concert series, and the branch hosts regular author talks, book discussions, and film screenings.

beats.script_body: One of the country's largest art museums, the Brooklyn Museum holds a world-class collection ranging from Egyptian mummies to contemporary art. Housed in a five-hundred-and-sixty-thousand-square-foot beaux arts building with a glass entrance pavilion, this venerable institution sits right beside the Brooklyn Botanic Garden and has been at the heart of Brooklyn's cultural life since 1823. Beyond five floors of permanent installations embracing the world's cultures, special exhibitions showcase rarely-seen items and the work of prominent artists such as Annie Leibovitz and Takashi Murakami.

In addition to five floors of permanent installations embracing the world's cultures, special exhibitions showcase items from the collection that are rarely seen, as well as the work of such prominent artists as Annie Leibovitz and Takashi Murakami.

beats.script_body: Central Park may be more famous, but Brooklynites are fiercely loyal to Prospect Park, a five-hundred-and-eighty-five-acre sweep of woods, hills, lakes, and waterfalls. Constructed by Central Park's own designers, Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, and opened in 1867, the park offers chances to relax, go boating, enjoy live music, and cozy up to farm animals. Scenic trails snake through the borough's only forest and pass a sixty-acre lake, and bird lovers are delighted by a two-hundred-species bird population that includes green herons and red-tailed hawks.

beats.script_body: Park Slope is well known for its stunning brownstones, popular music venues, and family-friendly eateries and stores. Seventh Avenue is one of its charming, café-lined thoroughfares, while side streets to the right lead toward Fifth Avenue, packed with new boutiques and restaurants. Al di La, an elegant Italian spot on Fifth Avenue, was one of the first restaurants to put Brooklyn on the culinary map, alongside standouts like Juventino's Mexican-inflected fare, Talde's inventive Pan-Asian menu, and the ultra-fresh seafood of Brooklyn Fish Camp.
